body.x: Most biodatas do not fail because the person is unsuitable. They fail because the document is hard to read, or missing the facts families screen for first. A receiving family typically gives a new biodata less than a minute before deciding whether it deserves a phone call. Your task is not to impress them in that minute. It is to make the minute easy: the right facts, in the order families look for them, written plainly.
What a biodata has to carry

Strip away every decorative format circulating on WhatsApp and a working biodata carries six blocks of information. First, identity: full name, age or date of birth, height if your community expects it, and current city and country — not just a hometown the family left decades ago. Second, religious practice, stated in the specifics Shia families actually ask about: daily prayers, fasting, hijab for a daughter, attendance at majalis, and the marja followed, where the family is comfortable naming one. Third, family: parents' names and occupations, siblings and their marital status, and the family's place of origin. Fourth, education and work: degrees with the institution's city, current role and employer type, and whether the work involves travel or relocation. Fifth, languages spoken at home — Urdu, Arabic, Farsi, Gujarati, English — because this quietly decides how two families will actually talk. Sixth, expectations: the age range, locations, and practice level being sought, plus any firm condition, stated once and without apology.

Notice what is missing from that list: a photograph pasted into the document itself, and references to income figures. Photographs travel separately, under the family's control, only when a conversation has genuinely started. Income belongs to a later, direct conversation, not to a file that may be forwarded further than you ever intended.
The order that earns a full reading

Families screen in a fixed sequence, and a good biodata respects it. They check the basics first — age, city, marital status — because a mismatch there ends the matter kindly and quickly. Then practice, because for most Shia families this is the true filter: not a claim of piety, but concrete habits they can picture. Then family background and origin, then education and work, and only at the end, expectations. When expectations appear at the top, even reasonable conditions read as demands. When the basics are buried in paragraph three, many readers never reach them. Put the screening facts in clean lines at the top, the human detail in short paragraphs beneath, and expectations last.
A worked example, piece by piece

The following example is fictional — the person does not exist — but every line is doing a job worth copying. The opening lines read: "Fatima Zahra, 26. Born and raised in Birmingham, UK. Never married." Three facts, no adjectives, and the three most common screening questions answered before the reader has scrolled. Compare the opening many biodatas use — a paragraph about being God-fearing and family-oriented — which answers nothing.

The practice section of the example reads: "Prays five times daily and fasts in Ramadan. Wears hijab. Attends majalis at the local centre, more regularly in Muharram and Ramadan. Family follows Ayatollah Sistani." Each sentence is checkable and concrete; there is no claim to be "very religious", a phrase that means something different in every house. The work section reads: "BSc Accounting, University of Birmingham. Audit associate at a mid-sized firm, training toward qualification. Based in Birmingham and not looking to relocate outside the UK." That last sentence will lose her some enquiries — and save her months of conversations that were never going to work.

The expectations close the document: "Seeking a practising Shia husband, 26–32, settled in the UK. Family involvement from the start is important to us." Short, warm, and complete. Nothing oversells — and that restraint is exactly why a family trusts it enough to respond.
The hard fields, handled with dignity

Three subjects make writers freeze: a previous marriage, a health condition, and a complicated work situation. The rule for all three is the same — state the fact plainly, once, without hiding it or apologising for it at length. A divorce is recorded with its basic shape: "Previously married; divorced in 2023; no children." A family that will reject this will reject it whenever they learn it, and learning it late — after meetings, after attachment — converts a simple no into a lasting grievance in a small community. Health matters that affect married life belong in the biodata in one factual line, with detail reserved for a serious conversation. A career gap reads far better as "Between roles since March; previously five years in logistics" than as a silence the reader is left to explain to themselves. Honesty early is not a disadvantage. In community searches, it is the whole of your reputation.

Salary figures, property details and anything that reads as a price tag
A long list of rejected categories — it tells readers more about temperament than about fit
Photographs embedded in the file, which strip you of control over where your image travels
Claims nobody can verify, such as being a hafiz or a sayyid, stated loosely — lineage and learning are checked in Shia communities, and an error here ends trust entirely
Referees' contact details, before anyone has agreed to be contacted
Forwarding etiquette: who sends, to whom, with what

A biodata should be sent by a parent, an elder sibling, or a named family representative — not broadcast by the person themselves to a list of strangers. Send it to one family at a time, or to a matchmaker who has agreed to hold it, and always with a short cover note that does three things: says who is sending and their relationship, says where the receiving family's name came from, and asks for a reply within a reasonable time, after which the senders will assume it is a no and move on without any hard feeling. That last sentence is a kindness in both directions; the silent, indefinite wait is one of the cruellest features of the rishta process. Finally, when a family says no, the biodata should not travel onward from them to a cousin, a friend, or a group chat. It was entrusted for one reading. On Shia Rishta, the same discipline is built into the format: profiles are shared through mutual interest, photographs stay private until the account holder shares them, and a wali or guardian can be part of the conversation from the start.

excerpt: A biodata gets about thirty seconds of attention before a family decides whether to read on — here is what to put in it, in what order, and how to handle the hard fields honestly.
title: How to write a Shia marriage biodata that gets responses
